newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean court issues warrants for strike leaders.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean court issues warrants for strike leaders.

text.p: Brushing aside the threat of all-out strikes and appeals by an international labour group, a South Korean court on Friday issued arrest warrants for seven strike leaders huddled in a Seoul cathedral.
Militant leaders of the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions have warned that any attempt to seize them will trigger nationwide work stoppages, including a public sector shutdown.
It was not immediately clear whether police would attempt to storm the grounds of Myongdong Cathedral, where the seven are sheltering in freezing conditions inside a ramshackle tent.
Earlier, confederation president Kwon Young-kil and six deputies rebuffed police trying to deliver a summons for them to appear in court.

State prosecutors had asked for the arrest of the seven on charges of obstructing business by staging illegal strikes over the introduction of a new labour law that allows worker layoffs for the first time.
The judge first said he wanted to question them but issued the warrants after they refused to show up.
Police investigators supported by several hundred riot police burst into confederation headquarters shortly before midnight on Thursday and carted away documents.
"If any of the seven, including myself, are arrested, we have orders to start intensive strikes immediately," Kwon told a news conference before the warrants were issued.

In the southeast city of Ulsan, a worker was in critical condition after setting fire to himself during a clash between strikers from the Hyundai Group and riot police, a Hyundai union official and hospital spokesman said.
Three others were hurt during the incident. It was the first serious injury reported since strikes erupted on December 26 when the labour bill was rammed through parliament.
Hyundai workers have been at the forefront of strikes that the confederation says has brought out 190,000 of its 500,000 members. The labour ministry says only 70,000 workers are out.
A Myongdong church official urged government and union leaders to compromise, saying "democracy is the result of talks and cooperation".
But Chang Bok-pil said there was nothing clergy could do if police decided to violate sacred ground and arrest the seven in their tent pitched beneath a statue of the Virgin Mary.

Leaders of the Brussels-based International Confederation of Free Trade Unions (ICFTU) were due to arrive on Saturday to try to persuade the government to scrap a law they say is a step towards greater repression.
The ICFTU has urged South Korea not to arrest the seven.
Minister for Labour Jin Nyum rejected ICFTU criticisms and said no other country had been awarding annual 15 percent pay increases while still suffering from violent industrial strife.
"There is no customer in the world who wants to buy products out of plants where petrol bombs fly because of violent labour disputes," he told a news conference.
"There is nothing in the new law that worsens the rights of workers."
The ICFTU filed a complaint with the International Labour Organisation about the law.
It objects to provisions allowing strikers to be replaced by outside workers, banning dismissed workers from belonging to unions and prohibiting companies from paying strikers.
Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung renewed warnings to strikers that they risked punishment.
"The government has no alternative but to take stern measures against illegal strikes for the sake of protecting public interests," Lee told businessmen.

Filipino workers picketed the South Korean embassy in Manila. "We are here to support the struggle of the working class in South Korea," said Manuel Sarmiento, Secretary-General of the May First Movement.
South Korean's largest union body, the Federation of Korean Trade Unions, has called on workers to join the biggest strike in the nation's history for two days starting next Tuesday.
